distractorExplanations.c: The mosaic theory covers public and nonmaterial nonpublic pieces; a pending 30% tender premium is material by itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Seeking confirmation does not make the information public; trading would still be acting on material nonpublic information.

prompt: Ellen Vance, CFA, manages pension accounts and directs client trades to a broker that charges higher commissions in exchange for soft-dollar credits. Which use of those credits is consistent with Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care?

options.text: Paying for travel to a conference unrelated to the accounts' holdings
Paying for new office furniture for the portfolio management team
Paying for a marketing database used to win new institutional clients
Paying for third-party equity research used to manage those accounts

explanation: Under Standard III(A), brokerage commissions belong to the client. Soft dollars may be used only for research and services that directly assist the manager's investment decisions for those clients; furniture, marketing, or unrelated travel benefit the firm instead.

distractorExplanations.a: Expenses that do not assist the investment decision-making for those clients are not permissible uses of client commissions.
distractorExplanations.b: Furniture benefits the manager, not the clients whose commissions paid for it; soft dollars must buy research that aids the client.
distractorExplanations.c: Client brokerage is client property; using it to market the firm puts the manager's interest ahead of clients'.

prompt: During a portfolio review, Ravi Shah, CFA, learns that a long-time client is routing money from an undisclosed business through the account in a way Shah believes is illegal. Under Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, Shah:

options.text: May disclose the information to the proper authorities
Must first obtain the client's written consent before telling anyone
Must keep the information secret because it concerns a current client
May share the details with other clients so they can protect themselves

explanation: Standard III(E) requires members to keep client information confidential unless it concerns illegal activities by the client, disclosure is required by law, or the client permits it. Suspected money laundering falls under the illegal-activity exception, and local law may even require reporting.

distractorExplanations.b: Consent is required for ordinary disclosures, not when the information concerns the client's illegal activity.
distractorExplanations.c: Confidentiality does not protect information about illegal activities by the client; disclosure to authorities is permitted.
distractorExplanations.d: The exception covers disclosure to proper authorities, not spreading client information to third parties.

prompt: A wealthy client tells Mei Lin, CFA, a portfolio manager at Corbel Advisers, that he will give her a personal $20,000 bonus if his account beats its benchmark by two percentage points this year. Under Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements, Lin should:

options.text: Obtain written consent from Corbel before accepting the arrangement
Decline, because CFA members may never accept bonuses from clients
Accept it, since the client chose the target and she will disclose it to him
Accept it, as long as she treats the client the same as other clients

explanation: Standard IV(B) requires members to obtain written consent from all parties involved, chiefly the employer, before accepting compensation or benefits that could compete with or create a conflict with the employer's interests, such as a performance bonus from a client.

distractorExplanations.b: Client bonuses are not banned outright; they are permitted when the employer gives written consent after full disclosure.
distractorExplanations.c: The client already knows; the duty under IV(B) is to the employer, who must consent in writing to outside compensation.
distractorExplanations.d: Fair treatment of clients is a separate duty; it does not replace the employer's written consent to the arrangement.

prompt: Gwen Ortiz, CFA, is promoted to head of trading at a firm whose compliance system has no pre-clearance for personal trades and no trade-allocation procedure. Senior management will not fund improvements this year. Under Standard IV(C), Ortiz should:

options.text: Report the firm to CFA Institute and resign immediately
Decline supervisory duties in writing until adequate procedures exist
Accept the role, because the compliance system is senior management's duty
Accept the role and rely on staff reporting violations voluntarily

explanation: Under Standard IV(C), members with supervisory responsibility must make reasonable efforts to ensure compliance. If the firm's compliance procedures are inadequate and cannot be fixed, the member should decline in writing to accept supervisory responsibility until reasonable procedures are adopted.

distractorExplanations.a: Resignation and reporting are not required first steps; the guidance is to decline supervision in writing and document it.
distractorExplanations.c: Supervisors must make reasonable efforts to detect and prevent violations; an inadequate system leaves her unable to do so.
distractorExplanations.d: A supervisor cannot discharge the duty by relying on voluntary reporting when the firm lacks a reasonable compliance system.

prompt: In a client report, analyst Hugo Petit, CFA, writes: "Aster Motors will earn $3.10 per share next year, and the stock will reach $60." Both figures come from his own model. Under Standard V(B) Communication with Clients, the main problem is that Petit:

options.text: Publishes an EPS forecast, which is prohibited without management approval
Uses a one-year horizon, which is too short for a buy recommendation
Gives a price target without disclosing his personal trading history
Presents his own forecasts as facts rather than as opinions

explanation: Standard V(B) requires members to distinguish between fact and opinion in investment analysis and recommendations. Model-based EPS and price targets are opinions; stating them as certainties misleads clients about the uncertainty in the recommendation.

distractorExplanations.a: Analysts may publish their own forecasts; they must simply identify them as estimates or opinions.
distractorExplanations.b: No Standard sets a minimum forecast horizon; the wording, not the horizon, is the violation.
distractorExplanations.c: Personal holdings belong under conflict disclosure in VI(A); the V(B) issue here is fact versus opinion.

prompt: Carla Duarte, CFA, is about to publish a buy recommendation on Pinecrest Bank. Her husband sits on Pinecrest's board, and her household owns a small amount of Pinecrest stock. Under Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts, Duarte should:

options.text: Sell the household's shares, after which no disclosure is needed
Disclose only the shareholding, because the board seat is her husband's
Disclose nothing, since the holding is small relative to her net worth
Disclose both the board seat and the holding in her research report

explanation: Standard VI(A) requires full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably impair independence and objectivity, including beneficial ownership and family relationships such as a spouse's directorship. Disclosure lets clients weigh the recommendation knowing the conflicts.

distractorExplanations.a: Selling removes one conflict, but the spouse's board seat still has to be disclosed to clients and her employer.
distractorExplanations.b: Conflicts held by immediate family, such as a spouse's directorship, can impair objectivity and must be disclosed too.
distractorExplanations.c: Materiality to her finances is not the test; the relationship could reasonably be expected to affect her objectivity.

prompt: Owen Blake, CFA, a financial planner, has agreed to receive $500 from a local accounting firm for each client he refers there. A new prospect asks Blake to recommend a tax accountant. Under Standard VI(C) Referral Fees, Blake must:

options.text: Disclose the fee to his employer only, since the client pays nothing extra
Stop accepting the fee, because referral fees are prohibited by the Standards
Tell the prospect about the $500 fee before she engages the accountant
Tell the prospect about the fee only if she later signs with the accountant

explanation: Standard VI(C) requires members to disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients any compensation, consideration, or benefit received for recommending products or services, before the client or prospect enters into an agreement.

distractorExplanations.a: Clients and prospects must also be told, even if the fee does not raise the price they pay.
distractorExplanations.b: Referral fees are permitted; the requirement is disclosure to the employer, clients, and prospects.
distractorExplanations.d: Disclosure must come before the client enters the engagement so she can judge the recommendation's objectivity.

prompt: When presenting a large-cap composite to prospects, Sofia Lund, CFA, removes the three accounts that clients closed after poor results, saying they no longer exist. The remaining accounts show a five-year return 1.8% above the benchmark. Under Standard III(D) Performance Presentation, this is:

options.text: A violation only if the firm claims compliance with GIPS
Acceptable, provided she labels the results as unaudited
Acceptable, because only current clients' results are relevant to prospects
A violation, because dropping closed accounts creates survivorship bias

explanation: Standard III(D) requires fair, accurate, and complete performance presentation. Dropping accounts that terminated after poor results inflates the composite through survivorship bias. Terminated portfolios must stay in the historical record for the periods they were managed.

distractorExplanations.a: III(D) applies to all members whether or not the firm claims GIPS compliance; misleading performance is prohibited.
distractorExplanations.b: Labeling does not cure a misleading composite; the excluded losers make the record unfair and incomplete.
distractorExplanations.c: Excluding closed accounts overstates the composite's record; past performance must include accounts that later terminated.

prompt: Right after sitting Level I, a candidate posts on an online forum that the exam "had four questions on duration and convexity, including one on effective convexity for a callable bond." Under Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs, this post is:

options.text: A violation only if the candidate quotes an exam question word for word
Acceptable, because general comments about exam difficulty are allowed
Acceptable, because the curriculum readings are already public
A violation, because it discloses specific topics and questions tested

explanation: Standard VII(A) prohibits conduct that compromises the integrity or validity of CFA Institute programs, including disclosing confidential exam information such as specific topics, question formats, or formulas tested. Candidates may only make general comments, for example that the exam was challenging.

distractorExplanations.a: Confidentiality is breached by revealing tested topics or formulas, even without quoting the question text.
distractorExplanations.b: Broad comments on difficulty are allowed, but naming specific topics and question details breaches exam confidentiality.
distractorExplanations.c: The curriculum is public, but which topics and question types appeared on the exam is confidential.

prompt: A company reports net income of $500,000 and depreciation of $80,000. During the year, accounts receivable rose by $40,000, inventory fell by $25,000, and accounts payable fell by $15,000. Using the indirect method, what is cash flow from operating activities?
explanation: CFO = net income + depreciation − increase in receivables + decrease in inventory − decrease in payables = 500,000 + 80,000 − 40,000 + 25,000 − 15,000 = $550,000. Increases in operating assets and decreases in operating liabilities consume cash.

distractorExplanations.a: Leaves out the $80,000 depreciation add-back; non-cash expenses reduce net income but not cash.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the $15,000 drop in payables as a cash inflow; paying down payables uses cash and is subtracted.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the $40,000 rise in receivables as an inflow; sales not yet collected must be subtracted.

prompt: On 1 January a software firm sells a bundle for $120,000: a perpetual license delivered immediately plus two years of support. Standalone prices are $100,000 for the license and $50,000 for the support. Under IFRS 15, how much revenue does the firm recognize in the first year?
explanation: Allocate the $120,000 by relative standalone selling prices: license 100/150 × 120,000 = $80,000 (recognized at delivery) and support 50/150 × 120,000 = $40,000 (recognized evenly over two years, $20,000 per year). Year-one revenue = 80,000 + 20,000 = $100,000.

distractorExplanations.a: Spreads the whole bundle evenly over two years; the license is a separate obligation satisfied at delivery.
distractorExplanations.b: Recognizes only the allocated license revenue and forgets the first year's share of support revenue.
distractorExplanations.d: Books the entire bundle at signing; support revenue must be recognized over the two-year service period.

prompt: An asset has a carrying amount of $900,000. Its undiscounted future cash flows are $950,000, its fair value is $770,000, costs to sell are $10,000, and its value in use is $820,000. What impairment loss is recognized under IFRS?
explanation: Under IFRS, recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs to sell ($760,000) and value in use ($820,000), so $820,000. The asset is impaired by 900,000 − 820,000 = $80,000. US GAAP would first test undiscounted cash flows ($950,000 > $900,000) and record no impairment.

distractorExplanations.a: Applies the US GAAP recoverability test with undiscounted cash flows; IFRS compares carrying amount with recoverable amount directly.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses carrying amount minus fair value, the US GAAP measurement step, rather than the IFRS recoverable amount.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses fair value less costs to sell ($760,000) even though the higher value in use sets the recoverable amount.

prompt: A company reports $200 million of bank debt, $100 million of bonds, and $100 million of lease liabilities, with total equity of $600 million. What is its debt-to-capital ratio including lease liabilities?
explanation: Total debt including leases = 200 + 100 + 100 = $400 million. Total capital = debt + equity = 400 + 600 = $1,000 million. Debt-to-capital = 400 / 1,000 = 40.0%. Analysts include lease liabilities because they are fixed financing obligations.

distractorExplanations.a: Divides debt excluding leases ($300 million) by capital that includes leases ($1,000 million), mixing the two definitions.
distractorExplanations.b: Excludes lease liabilities from both debt and capital; leases recognized on the balance sheet are debt-like obligations.
distractorExplanations.d: Computes debt-to-equity (400/600) rather than debt divided by total capital (debt plus equity).

prompt: A company earns net income of $1,000,000, pays $100,000 of preferred dividends, and has 500,000 common shares outstanding all year. Its preferred shares are convertible into 100,000 common shares. What is diluted EPS?
explanation: Basic EPS = (1,000,000 − 100,000) / 500,000 = $1.80. If converted, no preferred dividends are paid and shares rise to 600,000: diluted EPS = 1,000,000 / 600,000 = $1.67. Because $1.67 < $1.80, the security is dilutive and diluted EPS is $1.67.

distractorExplanations.a: Deducts the preferred dividends and also adds the conversion shares; under if-converted, the dividends are added back.
distractorExplanations.c: Reports basic EPS; the convertible is dilutive and must be included because $1.67 is below $1.80.
distractorExplanations.d: Ignores the preferred dividends and the conversion shares, dividing net income by basic shares only.

prompt: An analyst reviews a distributor whose sales grew 5% this year. Which observation is the strongest warning sign of aggressive revenue recognition, such as channel stuffing?

options.text: Days of sales outstanding rose from 45 to 70 days
Operating cash flow exceeded net income in each of the last three years
Capital expenditures were roughly equal to depreciation expense
Inventory turnover rose from 6.0 to 7.5 times

explanation: If receivables grow much faster than sales, so that DSO jumps from 45 to 70 days, revenue may be booked before customers are committed to pay, as in channel stuffing or bill-and-hold sales. The other observations are neutral or signs of good quality.

distractorExplanations.b: Cash flow consistently above earnings usually signals higher, not lower, earnings quality.
distractorExplanations.c: Capex near depreciation suggests maintenance spending, unrelated to how revenue is recognized.
distractorExplanations.d: Faster inventory turnover means goods sell more quickly, which does not by itself point to premature revenue.

prompt: Last year an IFRS reporter wrote inventory down from its $100,000 cost to its $80,000 net realizable value. The goods are still on hand, and net realizable value has now recovered to $95,000. How does the company account for the recovery?

options.text: Make no entry, because inventory write-downs can never be reversed
Record a $15,000 revaluation gain in other comprehensive income
Reverse $15,000 of the write-down, reducing cost of sales
Reverse the full $20,000, restoring the inventory to its original cost

explanation: IAS 2 requires inventory at the lower of cost and net realizable value. When NRV rises, the earlier write-down is reversed, capped at the original amount, so carrying value goes from $80,000 to $95,000 (still below the $100,000 cost) and the $15,000 reversal reduces cost of sales. US GAAP prohibits reversals.

distractorExplanations.a: That is the US GAAP rule; IFRS requires reversal up to the original write-down when NRV recovers.
distractorExplanations.b: Inventory recoveries go through profit or loss as lower cost of sales, not through OCI like PP&E revaluations.
distractorExplanations.d: Inventory is carried at the lower of cost and NRV; with NRV at $95,000, the reversal stops at $15,000.

prompt: An index holds two stocks. Stock A, with a $800 million market cap, returns +10% for the month; Stock B, with a $200 million market cap, returns −5%. What is the equal-weighted index return?
explanation: An equal-weighted index gives each constituent the same weight: (10% + (−5%)) / 2 = 2.5%. A cap-weighted index would return 0.8 × 10% + 0.2 × (−5%) = 7.0%; the gap shows how weighting drives index returns.

distractorExplanations.b: Adds the two returns (10% − 5%) without averaging them; equal weighting divides by the number of stocks.
distractorExplanations.c: Computes the market-cap-weighted return (0.8 × 10% + 0.2 × −5%) instead of the equal-weighted one.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses cap weights and treats B's −5% as a gain (0.8 × 10% + 0.2 × 5%), getting the sign wrong.

prompt: Which industry feature most likely gives existing companies the strongest pricing power, according to Porter's five forces?

options.text: A few large customers that buy a big share of industry output
Slow industry growth combined with high fixed costs and exit barriers
Many similar-sized competitors selling an undifferentiated product
High switching costs for customers and strong brand loyalty

explanation: Porter's framework links pricing power to weak competitive forces. High switching costs and brand loyalty reduce the threat of substitutes and new entrants and lower buyer power, letting incumbents sustain prices. The other features strengthen rivalry or buyer power.

distractorExplanations.a: Concentrated buyers have strong bargaining power and can push prices down.
distractorExplanations.b: Slow growth and high fixed costs push firms to cut prices to fill capacity, increasing rivalry.
distractorExplanations.c: Fragmented rivalry with commodity products intensifies price competition and weakens pricing power.

prompt: A stock will pay dividends of $1.00 in one year and $1.20 in two years. After that, dividends will grow at 4% per year forever. The required return is 10%. What is the stock's value today?

distractorExplanations.a: Values the year-2 terminal price as D2/(r − g) = $20.00 instead of D3/(r − g), using the wrong dividend.
distractorExplanations.c: Discounts the $20.80 terminal value by only one year, although it is a price at the end of year 2.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the dividends and terminal value without discounting any of them to the present.

prompt: An investor owns a stock trading at $48 and wants an order that will sell automatically if the price falls to $40, to limit her losses. Which order should she place?

options.text: A stop order to sell at $40
A stop order to buy at $40
A market-on-close order to sell
A limit order to sell at $40

explanation: A sell stop order sits below the current price and becomes a market order once the price trades at or through the stop, here $40. It protects a long position against further declines, though in a fast market the execution price may be below $40.

distractorExplanations.b: Buy stops are placed above the market to cap losses on short positions, not to exit a long position.
distractorExplanations.c: This sells at today's close regardless of price; it does not wait for a fall to $40.
distractorExplanations.d: A sell limit at $40, below the market, would execute immediately near $48 rather than waiting for a decline.

prompt: A company has a $2,000 million market capitalization, $600 million of debt, $100 million of preferred stock, $50 million of noncontrolling interest, and $150 million of cash. What is its enterprise value?

options.text: $2,500 million
$2,600 million
$2,750 million
$2,900 million

explanation: EV = market value of equity + debt + preferred stock + noncontrolling interest − cash = 2,000 + 600 + 100 + 50 − 150 = $2,600 million. EV measures the value of the operating business to all capital providers.

distractorExplanations.a: Leaves out the preferred stock; preferred claims rank ahead of common and belong in enterprise value.
distractorExplanations.c: Fails to subtract cash; enterprise value nets out cash and short-term investments.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds cash instead of subtracting it, overstating the value of the operating business.

prompt: An investor sold short 1,000 shares of Ridgeway Inc. using borrowed shares. While the position is open, Ridgeway pays a $0.50 per share dividend. What happens?

options.text: The short seller must pay $500 to the lender of the shares
The short seller receives the $500 dividend because he sold the shares
The broker deducts the dividend from the lender's account
Nobody receives the dividend while the shares are on loan

explanation: A short seller must pay the lender of the securities any dividends or interest paid while the shares are borrowed (payments in lieu). Here that is 1,000 × $0.50 = $500, which reduces the short position's return.

distractorExplanations.b: The company pays the buyer who now holds the shares; the short seller owes the lender a matching amount.
distractorExplanations.c: The lender is made whole for the dividend; the cost falls on the short seller, not the lender.
distractorExplanations.d: The new owner receives the dividend from the company, and the lender is compensated by the short seller.

prompt: An investor buys a stock at $40 with 40% initial margin and borrows the rest at 6% a year. After one year she sells at $46, having received a $1 dividend. Ignoring commissions, what is her return on equity?
explanation: Per share: equity = 0.40 × 40 = $16; loan = $24; interest = 0.06 × 24 = $1.44. Return = (46 − 40 + 1 − 1.44) / 16 = 5.56 / 16 = 34.75%. Leverage magnifies the 17.5% unlevered return.

distractorExplanations.a: Computes the unlevered return (6 + 1)/40; with 40% margin her equity is only $16 per share.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaves out the $1 dividend while still deducting the $1.44 margin interest.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaves out the 6% interest on the $24 loan, overstating the leveraged return.

prompt: A bond with $1,000 par pays a 6% coupon semiannually. Using 30/360, 60 days have passed in the current 180-day coupon period, and the bond's flat (quoted) price is $985. What is its full price?
explanation: Semiannual coupon = 1,000 × 6% / 2 = $30. Accrued interest = 30 × 60/180 = $10. Full (dirty) price = flat price + accrued interest = 985 + 10 = $995.

distractorExplanations.a: Subtracts accrued interest from the flat price; the buyer pays the seller accrued interest on top of the quote.
distractorExplanations.b: Gives the flat price only; the full price adds the $10 of interest accrued since the last coupon.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the whole $30 semiannual coupon instead of the share accrued over 60 of 180 days.

prompt: A five-year bond with $1,000 par and a 7% annual coupon trades at $950. What is its current yield?
explanation: Current yield = annual coupon / price = 70 / 950 = 7.37%. It ignores the capital gain as the discount bond is pulled to par, which is why yield to maturity (about 8.2%) is higher.

distractorExplanations.a: Multiplies the coupon rate by the price (0.07 × 950 / 1,000) instead of dividing the coupon by the price.
distractorExplanations.b: Gives the coupon rate, which is based on par value, not the bond's market price.
distractorExplanations.d: Approximates the yield to maturity by adding the discount's amortization; current yield ignores the pull to par.

prompt: A portfolio holds bonds with a full market value of $1,020,000 and a modified duration of 6.0. What is the portfolio's price value of a basis point (PVBP)?
explanation: PVBP = full value × modified duration × 0.0001 = 1,020,000 × 6.0 × 0.0001 = $612. It estimates the dollar price change for a one basis point change in yield.

distractorExplanations.a: Shifts the decimal one place; one basis point is 0.0001, so PVBP = 1,020,000 × 6.0 × 0.0001.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses the $1,000,000 par amount instead of the $1,020,000 full market value.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses a 10 basis point change (0.001) rather than a single basis point.

prompt: Harlow Industries files for bankruptcy. Which of its creditors ranks first for repayment from the assets pledged as collateral?

options.text: Its first-lien secured term lenders
Holders of its senior unsecured notes
Holders of its second-lien secured notes
Holders of its subordinated debentures

explanation: Priority of claims in bankruptcy runs: first-lien (senior secured) debt, second-lien secured debt, senior unsecured, senior subordinated, subordinated, and junior subordinated debt, then preferred and common equity. First-lien holders have the first claim on the pledged assets.

distractorExplanations.b: Senior unsecured debt ranks below all secured debt for the value of the pledged collateral.
distractorExplanations.c: Second-lien holders are paid from the collateral only after first-lien claims are satisfied in full.
distractorExplanations.d: Subordinated debt ranks below both secured and senior unsecured debt in the priority of claims.

prompt: A dealer finances $10,000,000 of Treasury collateral with a 30-day repurchase agreement at a 4% annual repo rate (360-day basis). The lender applies a 2% haircut. How much repo interest does the dealer pay?
explanation: Cash lent = 10,000,000 × (1 − 0.02) = $9,800,000. Repo interest = 9,800,000 × 0.04 × 30/360 = $32,667. The haircut protects the lender against a fall in collateral value.

distractorExplanations.a: Charges interest only on the $200,000 haircut, which is the part the lender does not finance.
distractorExplanations.c: Ignores the 2% haircut; the cash lent is $9,800,000, not the full $10,000,000 collateral value.
distractorExplanations.d: Charges a full year of interest instead of 30/360 of the annual repo rate.

prompt: The government yield curve slopes upward, but surveys show investors expect short-term rates to stay roughly unchanged. Which term structure theory best explains this combination?

options.text: Local expectations theory, because all bonds earn the risk-free rate over long horizons
Segmented markets theory, because short and long rates are driven by the same investors
Pure expectations theory, because forward rates equal expected future spot rates
Liquidity preference theory, because investors demand a term premium

explanation: Liquidity preference theory says investors require a risk (term) premium for holding longer maturities, so the yield curve can slope upward even when short rates are expected to stay flat. Pure expectations theory would predict a flat curve in that case.

distractorExplanations.a: Local expectations holds only for short holding periods; it does not explain a persistent upward slope.
distractorExplanations.b: Segmented markets assumes separate investor groups in each maturity, not the same investors across the curve.
distractorExplanations.c: Under pure expectations, flat rate expectations imply a flat curve; an upward slope would need rising expected rates.

prompt: A callable bond trades at 104. Its yield to maturity is 4.6%, its yield to first call (in two years) is 3.1%, and its yield to the second call date (in four years) is 3.9%. What is its yield to worst?
explanation: Yield to worst is the lowest of the yield to maturity and the yields to each call date: min(4.6%, 3.1%, 3.9%) = 3.10%. Premium callable bonds are at risk of being called at the earliest date.

distractorExplanations.b: Averages the two yields to call; yield to worst is the lowest single yield across call dates and maturity.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses the second call date, but the first call date produces a lower yield and is therefore the worst case.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses yield to maturity, which overstates the yield on a premium bond likely to be called early.

prompt: Stock X has a 45% standard deviation and a beta of 0.6. Stock Y has a 25% standard deviation and a beta of 1.3. Under the CAPM, which statement is correct?

options.text: Y has the higher expected return because it carries more systematic risk
X has the higher expected return because its unsystematic risk cannot be diversified
X has the higher expected return because its total risk is higher
Both have the same expected return because both are fairly priced

explanation: Under the CAPM, expected return depends only on beta (systematic risk): E(R) = Rf + β[E(Rm) − Rf]. Y's beta of 1.3 exceeds X's 0.6, so Y has the higher required return even though X's total standard deviation is larger.

distractorExplanations.b: Unsystematic risk is exactly the part a diversified investor can eliminate, so it is not rewarded.
distractorExplanations.c: Total risk includes diversifiable risk, which earns no premium; CAPM prices only beta.
distractorExplanations.d: Fair pricing means each sits on the security market line, at different returns set by their betas.

prompt: The risk-free rate is 3%. A risky portfolio has an expected return of 11% and a standard deviation of 20%. An investor wants a total standard deviation of 12% by combining the risky portfolio with the risk-free asset. What is her expected return?
explanation: On the capital allocation line, weight in the risky portfolio = 12% / 20% = 0.60. Expected return = 3% + 0.60 × (11% − 3%) = 3% + 4.8% = 7.8%. Equivalently, 0.60 × 11% + 0.40 × 3% = 7.8%.

distractorExplanations.a: Applies the 60% weight to the risky return but leaves out the risk-free return on the other 40%.
distractorExplanations.c: Multiplies the weight by the full 11% risky return instead of the 8% risk premium before adding Rf.
distractorExplanations.d: Inverts the weight (20/12 instead of 12/20), which implies borrowing to lever up.

prompt: Which item in a client's investment policy statement is a constraint rather than an objective?

options.text: She needs $50,000 in cash next year for her daughter's tuition
She requires an after-tax return of 6% per year to fund retirement
She is willing to accept a 15% decline in a bad year
She wants the portfolio to beat inflation by 3% over the long run

explanation: IPS objectives cover return and risk. Constraints are liquidity, time horizon, tax concerns, legal and regulatory factors, and unique circumstances. A known $50,000 cash need next year is a liquidity constraint.

distractorExplanations.b: A required return is a return objective; constraints limit how the objectives can be met.
distractorExplanations.c: Willingness to bear losses describes risk tolerance, which is part of the risk objective.
distractorExplanations.d: A real return target is a return objective, not a constraint on the portfolio.

prompt: A fund reports a one-day 5% value at risk (VaR) of $2 million. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: The most the fund can lose in a single day is $2 million
The fund's average daily loss on bad days is $2 million
On 5% of days, the fund should expect to lose at least $2 million
There is a 95% probability that the fund will lose $2 million tomorrow

explanation: A one-day 5% VaR of $2 million means there is a 5% probability of a loss of at least $2 million over one day, or equivalently 95% confidence that the loss will be less. VaR says nothing about how large tail losses can get.

distractorExplanations.a: VaR is a threshold, not a maximum; losses beyond $2 million occur on the worst 5% of days.
distractorExplanations.b: The average loss in the tail is expected shortfall (CVaR), which exceeds VaR.
distractorExplanations.d: The 95% applies to losses smaller than $2 million, not to a loss of exactly that size.

prompt: A portfolio returned 12% last year with a beta of 1.1. The risk-free rate was 3% and the market returned 10%. What is the portfolio's Jensen's alpha?
explanation: CAPM-required return = 3% + 1.1 × (10% − 3%) = 10.7%. Jensen's alpha = actual − required = 12% − 10.7% = 1.30%. A positive alpha means the manager beat the return justified by the portfolio's systematic risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Multiplies beta by the total market return (1.1 × 10%) instead of by the market risk premium plus Rf.
distractorExplanations.c: Compares the portfolio with the market return directly, ignoring its beta and the risk-free rate.
distractorExplanations.d: Gives the CAPM-required return itself, not the difference between the actual and required return.

prompt: A fund manager invests only in the companies with the highest ESG ratings within each sector while keeping sector weights close to the benchmark. Which ESG investing approach is this?

options.text: Positive (best-in-class) screening
Negative screening of controversial industries
Shareholder engagement with low-rated companies
Thematic investing in sustainability themes

explanation: Positive or best-in-class screening selects the companies with the strongest ESG performance relative to peers in each sector, so the portfolio can stay sector-neutral. Negative screening excludes, and thematic investing tilts toward themes.

distractorExplanations.b: Negative screening excludes sectors or companies by criteria; this manager keeps all sectors and picks leaders.
distractorExplanations.c: Engagement uses ownership rights to influence companies, not a rule for which companies to hold.
distractorExplanations.d: Thematic investing targets specific themes such as clean energy, which changes sector exposure.

prompt: Historically, 30% of fund managers outperform. A screening model flags 80% of future outperformers and also flags 20% of managers who go on to underperform. If a manager is flagged, what is the probability that she will outperform?

distractorExplanations.a: Gives the joint probability of being flagged and outperforming (0.30 × 0.80), not the conditional one.
distractorExplanations.b: Gives the overall probability of being flagged (0.24 + 0.14), the denominator of Bayes' formula.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses P(flag | outperform) with P(outperform | flag); Bayes' formula reverses the conditioning.

prompt: Asset A has a standard deviation of 20% and Asset B a standard deviation of 30%. Their correlation is 0.5. What is the covariance of their returns?
explanation: Covariance = correlation × σA × σB = 0.5 × 0.20 × 0.30 = 0.0300. Covariance has squared units; dividing it back by the two standard deviations recovers the 0.5 correlation.

distractorExplanations.a: Squares the correlation (0.25 × 0.20 × 0.30); covariance uses the correlation itself.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaves out the correlation and multiplies the standard deviations only (0.20 × 0.30).
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the standard deviations and multiplies by the correlation (0.5 × 0.50).

prompt: A lease requires five annual payments of $1,000, with the first payment due today. At a 6% discount rate, what is the present value of the payments?
explanation: PV of an ordinary annuity = 1,000 × [1 − 1.06⁻⁵] / 0.06 = $4,212.36. Because payments come at the start of each year (annuity due), multiply by 1.06: 4,212.36 × 1.06 = $4,465.11.

distractorExplanations.a: Discounts the ordinary annuity value one more period instead of compounding it forward one period.
distractorExplanations.b: Values an ordinary annuity with payments at year-end; here the first payment is due today.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the payments without discounting them for the time value of money.

prompt: An investor wants to minimize the probability that her annual return falls below 3%. Portfolio A has an expected return of 9% and a standard deviation of 12%; Portfolio B has an expected return of 7% and a standard deviation of 6%. Using Roy's safety-first criterion, she should choose:

options.text: A, because its safety-first ratio is 0.75 versus 0.67 for B
Either one, because both have the same probability of returning below 3%
A, because its expected return is two percentage points higher
B, because its safety-first ratio is 0.67 versus 0.50 for A

explanation: Roy's SFRatio = (E[R] − R_L)/σ. A: (9 − 3)/12 = 0.50. B: (7 − 3)/6 = 0.67. Under normality, the higher ratio means a lower probability of a return below the 3% threshold, so choose B.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses E[R]/σ for A (9/12) and forgets to subtract the 3% threshold from the expected return.
distractorExplanations.b: The ratios differ (0.50 vs 0.67), so B has a lower probability of a shortfall below 3%.
distractorExplanations.c: Safety-first ranks by (E[R] − threshold) / σ, not expected return; A's ratio is only (9 − 3)/12 = 0.50.

prompt: The distribution of a fund's monthly returns is positively skewed and unimodal. Which relationship among its mean, median, and mode is most likely?

options.text: Mean > median > mode
Mode > median > mean
Mean, median, and mode are equal
Median > mean > mode

explanation: In a positively skewed distribution, a few large gains form a long right tail. The mean is pulled the most toward that tail, the median less, and the mode sits at the peak, so mean > median > mode.

distractorExplanations.b: This ordering describes a negatively skewed distribution with a long left tail.
distractorExplanations.c: Equality of the three measures holds for symmetric distributions, not skewed ones.
distractorExplanations.d: The mean is pulled furthest toward the long right tail, so it should exceed the median.

prompt: The spot rate is 1.1000 USD/EUR (US dollars per euro). The one-year interest rate is 5% in the United States and 3% in the euro area. What is the one-year forward rate implied by covered interest rate parity?

options.text: 1.0790 USD/EUR
1.1000 USD/EUR
1.1214 USD/EUR
1.1330 USD/EUR

explanation: Covered interest parity: F = S × (1 + i_price) / (1 + i_base) = 1.1000 × 1.05 / 1.03 = 1.1214 USD/EUR. The euro trades at a forward premium because euro interest rates are lower than US rates.

distractorExplanations.a: Inverts the interest rate ratio (1.03/1.05); the price currency's rate goes in the numerator.
distractorExplanations.b: Assumes the forward equals spot, ignoring the interest rate differential.
distractorExplanations.d: Grows the spot rate by the euro rate only (1.1000 × 1.03) instead of the rate ratio.

prompt: An economist wants a leading indicator to anticipate turning points in the business cycle. Which series is most appropriate?

options.text: New residential building permits
Average duration of unemployment
The average bank prime lending rate
Industrial production

explanation: Leading indicators such as building permits, average weekly manufacturing hours, new orders, and stock prices tend to turn before the overall economy. Coincident indicators move with it, and lagging indicators turn afterward.

distractorExplanations.b: Unemployment duration is a lagging indicator that turns after the economy does.
distractorExplanations.c: The prime rate is a lagging indicator that responds to earlier changes in activity.
distractorExplanations.d: Industrial production is a coincident indicator that moves with the cycle, not ahead of it.

prompt: In an economy, the marginal propensity to consume is 0.8 and the income tax rate is 25%. What is the fiscal multiplier on government spending?
explanation: Fiscal multiplier = 1 / [1 − MPC × (1 − t)] = 1 / [1 − 0.8 × 0.75] = 1 / 0.40 = 2.50. Taxes reduce the share of each extra dollar of income that is re-spent.

distractorExplanations.a: Multiplies the result by the MPC (0.8 × 2.5), which is closer to a tax-change multiplier.
distractorExplanations.c: Computes MPC / (1 − MPC) = 0.8/0.2, ignoring taxes and using the wrong formula.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses 1 / (1 − MPC) and ignores the tax rate that leaks income out of each spending round.

prompt: A country with a floating exchange rate and high capital mobility cuts interest rates sharply. Under the Mundell–Fleming model, the most likely effect is:

options.text: Capital inflows appreciate the currency and reduce net exports
No change in the currency, because rates do not affect capital flows
The currency appreciates because lower rates boost economic growth
Capital outflows depreciate the currency and raise net exports

explanation: With floating rates and mobile capital, monetary easing lowers the domestic interest rate, capital flows abroad, and the currency depreciates. A weaker currency makes exports cheaper, reinforcing the stimulus through higher net exports.

distractorExplanations.a: Lower domestic rates make the country's assets less attractive, so capital flows out, not in.
distractorExplanations.b: With high capital mobility, interest rate differentials drive capital flows and the exchange rate.
distractorExplanations.c: Any growth effect is outweighed by the capital outflow, which pushes the currency down.

prompt: A small country that cannot affect world prices imposes a tariff on imported steel. Which outcome is most likely in its domestic steel market?

options.text: Foreign producers pay the whole tariff by cutting their export prices
National welfare rises because tariff revenue exceeds consumer losses
Domestic consumption rises because imported steel becomes cheaper
Domestic production rises and the country suffers a deadweight loss

explanation: A tariff raises the domestic price by the tariff amount. Domestic producers expand output, consumers buy less, imports fall, and the government collects revenue, but the loss in consumer surplus exceeds these gains, leaving a deadweight loss for a small country.

distractorExplanations.a: A small country is a price taker; the world price is unchanged, so domestic buyers bear the tariff.
distractorExplanations.b: For a small country, consumer losses exceed the gains to producers and the government.
distractorExplanations.c: A tariff raises the domestic price of imports, so consumption falls rather than rises.

prompt: A limited partner is comparing two private equity funds with identical terms except the distribution waterfall. Which waterfall is generally more favorable to limited partners?

options.text: A waterfall with no clawback provision
A European (whole-of-fund) waterfall
A waterfall with a 100% GP catch-up and no hurdle
An American (deal-by-deal) waterfall

explanation: Under a European (whole-of-fund) waterfall, the GP receives carried interest only after LPs have received all contributed capital plus any preferred return for the whole fund. American deal-by-deal waterfalls pay carry earlier and depend on clawbacks to protect LPs.

distractorExplanations.a: Without a clawback, LPs cannot recover excess carry paid to the GP if later deals lose money.
distractorExplanations.c: A full catch-up with no hurdle accelerates GP carry and gives LPs no preferred return first.
distractorExplanations.d: Deal-by-deal waterfalls let the GP earn carry on early winners before LPs recover all contributed capital.

prompt: Over one year, a fully collateralized long commodity futures position has a spot price return of +4%, a roll yield of −2%, and a collateral yield of 3%. What is its total return?
explanation: Total return on a collateralized futures position = spot return + roll return + collateral return = 4% + (−2%) + 3% = 5%. Negative roll yield arises when expiring contracts are rolled into more expensive later ones.

distractorExplanations.a: Subtracts the collateral yield as a cost; a fully collateralized position earns interest on its cash.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaves out the 3% collateral yield earned on the cash held to back the futures position.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaves out the negative roll yield from rolling contracts in a contango market.

prompt: An office building generates $1.5 million of gross rental income, $0.3 million of operating expenses, and $0.4 million of annual mortgage payments. The market cap rate is 6%. What is its value using direct capitalization?

options.text: $13.3 million
$20.0 million
$25.0 million
$26.7 million

explanation: NOI = gross income − operating expenses = 1.5 − 0.3 = $1.2 million. Value = NOI / cap rate = 1.2 / 0.06 = $20.0 million. Debt service is excluded from NOI so the value reflects the property, not its financing.

distractorExplanations.a: Deducts the mortgage payments; NOI is measured before debt service, which depends on financing.
distractorExplanations.c: Capitalizes gross income instead of net operating income after operating expenses.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the mortgage payments back to NOI, double-counting cash that goes to the lender.

prompt: Acquirer Corp announces a stock-for-stock takeover of Target Inc. A merger arbitrage hedge fund will most likely:

options.text: Buy both companies' shares to profit from the deal's synergies
Short Target shares and buy Acquirer shares in the exchange ratio
Buy Target shares only, since stock deals carry no completion risk
Buy Target shares and short Acquirer shares in the exchange ratio

explanation: In a stock-for-stock deal, merger arbitrage buys the target and shorts the acquirer at the exchange ratio, locking in the spread between the target's price and the offer's value. The main risk is that the deal fails and the spread widens.

distractorExplanations.a: Merger arbitrage hedges market exposure; it does not take an outright long position in both firms.
distractorExplanations.b: This reverses the trade; the spread is earned by buying the target, which trades below the offer value.
distractorExplanations.c: Stock deals still carry completion risk, and the acquirer short hedges the value of the stock offered.

prompt: A distributed ledger network replaces proof of work with proof of stake. What is the main change in how blocks are validated?

options.text: Miners compete to solve hash puzzles using computing power
A central administrator approves every transaction before it posts
Every node must hold an equal number of coins to validate blocks
Validators are chosen in proportion to the coins they have staked

explanation: Under proof of stake, validators lock up (stake) coins and are selected to validate blocks roughly in proportion to their stake; dishonest validators can lose staked coins. Proof of work instead rewards miners who solve computational puzzles.

distractorExplanations.a: That describes proof of work, the energy-intensive mechanism being replaced here.
distractorExplanations.b: Central approval describes a permissioned, centralized system rather than a consensus mechanism.
distractorExplanations.c: Proof of stake does not require equal holdings; selection weight rises with the amount staked.

prompt: A company has sales of $10 million, variable costs of $6 million, and fixed operating costs of $2.5 million. If sales rise by 10%, by how much will operating income (EBIT) most likely increase?
explanation: Contribution margin = 10 − 6 = $4 million; EBIT = 4 − 2.5 = $1.5 million. Degree of operating leverage = CM / EBIT = 4 / 1.5 = 2.67. A 10% rise in sales raises EBIT by about 2.67 × 10% = 26.7%.

distractorExplanations.a: Assumes EBIT grows in line with sales; fixed costs make EBIT grow faster than sales.
distractorExplanations.b: Divides contribution margin by fixed costs (4.0/2.5) instead of by EBIT to get leverage.
distractorExplanations.d: Divides sales by EBIT (10/1.5); operating leverage uses contribution margin, not sales.

prompt: A highly leveraged company close to financial distress approves a very risky project with a negative NPV but a small chance of a large payoff. Which stakeholder conflict does this decision best illustrate?

options.text: Shareholders shifting risk onto the company's creditors
Managers building empires at shareholders' expense
Customers demanding lower prices from the company
Controlling shareholders exploiting minority shareholders

explanation: Near distress, equity holders gain most of the upside of a risky bet while creditors bear most of the downside. Choosing a risky negative-NPV project transfers value from creditors to shareholders, a classic shareholder–creditor conflict.

distractorExplanations.b: Empire building is a manager-shareholder conflict over size; here the risk shift benefits equity holders.
distractorExplanations.c: Customer relations are a separate stakeholder issue unrelated to project risk and the capital structure.
distractorExplanations.d: That conflict is between two classes of equity holders, not between equity and debt holders.

prompt: A supplier offers terms of 2/10, net 40. Using a 365-day year and compounding, what is the effective annual cost of not taking the discount and paying on day 40?
explanation: The cost of 30 extra days of credit is 2/98 = 2.04%. Effective annual cost = (1 + 0.02/0.98)^(365/30) − 1 = 1.0204^12.17 − 1 = 27.9%.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives the discount rate for one period, not the annualized cost of forgoing it.
distractorExplanations.b: Annualizes over the full 40 days (365/40); the extra credit lasts only 30 days.
distractorExplanations.c: Annualizes the 30-day cost by simple interest (2.04% × 365/30) instead of compounding.

prompt: Under Modigliani–Miller with corporate taxes, an unlevered firm is worth $500 million. It issues $200 million of perpetual debt and uses the proceeds to repurchase shares. The tax rate is 25%. What is the value of the levered firm?

options.text: $500 million
$550 million
$650 million
$700 million

explanation: MM Proposition I with taxes: V_L = V_U + t × D = 500 + 0.25 × 200 = $550 million. The gain comes from the present value of the interest tax shield on perpetual debt.

distractorExplanations.a: Applies MM without taxes; with corporate taxes, debt adds the value of the interest tax shield.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds after-tax debt (0.75 × 200); the tax shield is t × D, not (1 − t) × D.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the full $200 million of debt, as if borrowing itself created value.

prompt: An investor writes a put option with a $50 strike for a $4 premium. At expiration the stock trades at $43. What is her profit per share?
explanation: The put writer pays max(0, 50 − 43) = $7 at expiration and keeps the $4 premium. Profit = 4 − 7 = −$3 per share. Her breakeven is 50 − 4 = $46.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives the payoff she owes (50 − 43) and leaves out the $4 premium she received.
distractorExplanations.c: Gets the sign wrong; the put finishes $7 in the money, which outweighs the $4 premium.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the $4 premium to the $7 payoff; the writer owes the payoff, so the two must be netted.

prompt: An investor entered a one-year long forward on a non-dividend-paying stock at a forward price of $105. Six months later the stock trades at $110 and the annual risk-free rate is 5%. What is the value of the long forward?

distractorExplanations.a: A forward is worth zero only at initiation; after the price moves, it gains or loses value.
distractorExplanations.b: Compares the spot price with the forward price without discounting the $105 payment due in six months.
distractorExplanations.d: Discounts the forward price for a full year instead of the six months remaining.

prompt: A company has a floating-rate bank loan and wants to lock in its interest cost because it expects rates to rise. Which swap position should it enter?

options.text: Pay floating and receive floating at a different reference rate
Receive fixed and pay floating in an interest rate swap
Enter a currency swap that exchanges principal in two currencies
Pay fixed and receive floating in an interest rate swap

explanation: Paying fixed and receiving floating converts a floating-rate loan into a synthetic fixed-rate loan: the floating receipts offset the loan's floating payments, leaving a fixed net cost. If rates rise, the swap gains value as the floating leg increases.

distractorExplanations.a: A basis swap changes the floating benchmark but does not lock in a fixed rate.
distractorExplanations.b: This adds more floating exposure, so the company's costs would rise further if rates go up.
distractorExplanations.c: Currency swaps manage exchange-rate exposure, not the fixed-versus-floating mix of one loan.

prompt: All else equal, which change increases the value of a European put option on a non-dividend-paying stock?

options.text: A higher risk-free interest rate
A lower exercise price on the put
A higher price of the underlying stock
Higher volatility of the stock

explanation: Put value rises with volatility, because a wider spread of outcomes increases the chance of a large payoff while the loss is capped at the premium. Put value falls when the stock price rises, the strike falls, or the risk-free rate rises.

distractorExplanations.a: A higher rate lowers the present value of the strike received at exercise, reducing the put's value.
distractorExplanations.b: A lower strike lowers the payoff the put can deliver, reducing its value.
distractorExplanations.c: A put gains value as the stock falls; a higher stock price moves it toward out of the money.
